items.prompt: What is "sustainable boundary-setting" as this unit defines it?
choices: The practice of surfacing capacity limits as they're reached, so workload decisions get made deliberately instead of by default through silent overextension
The practice of refusing all new work requests as a fixed policy
A formal HR process for filing workload complaints
The practice of only ever working the exact hours listed in an employment contract
items.explanation: Sustainable boundary-setting is specifically about deliberate, visible trade-off decisions — not blanket refusal, HR processes, or rigid hour-counting.
items.reference:
👁️ Make the capacity limit visible and factual
🤝 Put the trade-off decision in the requester's hands

Why: the goal isn't refusing work — it's making sure new work gets added with an explicit, deliberate trade-off.

IsIsn't

items.prompt: What is "trade-off framing"?
choices: Presenting a new request alongside its real cost, rather than giving a flat yes or no
A negotiation tactic used exclusively in salary discussions
A framework for evaluating a company's overall business strategy
A method for splitting credit between team members on a shared project
items.explanation: Trade-off framing is specifically about surfacing the real cost of saying yes — not salary negotiation, business strategy, or credit-splitting.
items.reference:
① State the capacity signal
↓
② Offer the trade-off, not a flat answer
↓
③ Requester decides, with the real cost visible

Why: a flat yes or no skips the step where the real cost gets seen by the person who can actually weigh it.
items.learnMore:
Trade-off framing, laid out
New request arrives
↓
State current commitments (the capacity signal)
↓
Offer the trade-off: "I can take this on if X moves, or decline and keep X on track"
↓
Requester decides, with the real cost visible

The requester gets the decision because they usually hold the context — relative urgency — that the person raising the constraint doesn't.

Common mistake

Deciding unilaterally which existing commitment should slip, then only informing the requester afterward. That skips the one step — their actual say — that makes this fair.

② Usually means: needs more specific info to decide
↓
③ Repeat the specific trade-off, don't just give in

Why: giving in lets "urgent" quietly override the real constraint without anyone consciously deciding that was right.
items.learnMore:
What pushback usually means, and what it doesn't
ReadRight response
Manager needs more decision-making informationRepeat the specific trade-off, with the same named commitments
(Wrong read) the original framing was a mistakeCaving here lets urgency silently override the real constraint

Holding the trade-off under pushback isn't stubbornness — it keeps the decision honest and deliberate instead of letting pressure make it by default.

Common mistake

Treating any pushback as proof the original boundary was wrong, and abandoning it on the first repeat rather than giving the manager the information to actually decide.
